questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: India's water crisis is chiefly a failure of conservation and management rather than a shortage of rainfall.
Rainfall in India has been steadily declining over the decades.
Traditional water-harvesting methods are superior to all modern engineering solutions.
Cities should stop depending on groundwater altogether.
questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.passage: Water has always been treated as the one resource nature would never let us run short of. For centuries, rivers were diverted, wells were dug, and rains were awaited with quiet confidence that the cycle would repeat itself, generation after generation, without much effort on our part. That confidence is no longer warranted. Groundwater tables in large parts of the country have fallen by tens of metres within a single lifetime, and cities that once boasted of lakes and stepwells now import water by tanker in the summer months. The crisis is not one of absolute scarcity so much as of mismanagement: rainfall over a year, if captured and stored efficiently, would be more than adequate for most regions. What is missing is not water but the discipline to conserve it, the infrastructure to store it, and the will to price it so that it is neither wasted by the profligate nor denied to the poor. Traditional systems of water harvesting, dismissed as primitive by planners in the decades after independence, are being rediscovered today precisely because they solved, cheaply and locally, a problem that centralised piped supply has struggled to solve at scale. The lesson is an uncomfortable one for a civilisation enamoured of technological solutions: sometimes the answer lies not in inventing something new but in re-learning what was once common knowledge and needlessly abandoned.

questions.stem: The passage argues that effective military leadership is primarily built on:
options: Shared risk, competence under fire, and genuine concern for one's men, which together earn trust.
Strict enforcement of rank and hierarchy.
The ability to issue orders without being questioned.
Harsh discipline that leaves no room for dissent.
questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.passage: Leadership in uniform is often imagined as a matter of command: the ability to give an order and have it obeyed without question. This is a shallow reading of what makes an officer effective, particularly in conditions of extreme stress. Soldiers who have served under genuinely capable leaders describe something quite different from mere authority — they speak of an officer who ate what they ate, marched when they marched, and was seen forward of the position he was defending rather than behind it. Trust of this kind cannot be manufactured by rank alone; it is earned through a visible sharing of risk and hardship. Historians of warfare have long noted that units with the highest morale are rarely those with the harshest discipline, but those whose commanders demonstrated competence under fire and genuine concern for the welfare of their men. This does not mean that discipline is unimportant — an army without it dissolves into a mob — but that discipline sustained by fear is brittle, while discipline sustained by respect endures the worst that a battlefield can offer. The finest military traditions, across very different armies and eras, converge on this single insight: command is granted by rank, but leadership must be earned afresh, every single day, in the eyes of those who are asked to follow.

questions.stem: What does the passage suggest about how soldiers typically remember the outcome of a battle?
options: As an inevitable result decided long before the fighting began.
As something they rarely think about afterwards.
As a matter decided by a series of small, uncertain moments rather than any predetermined outcome.
As entirely determined by which side had more soldiers.
questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.passage: It is easy, looking back at a war from the safety of decades, to imagine that victory was inevitable and defeat foreordained. Soldiers who actually fought rarely describe it that way. What they remember, more often, is a string of moments in which the outcome hung on something as small as a signal received a few minutes late, a bridge held one hour longer than planned, or a reserve company committed at exactly the right time instead of five minutes too soon. Military historians have a name for this: the fog of war, the simple fact that no commander, however brilliant, ever has complete information about what is happening even a few kilometres away. Plans drawn up with perfect clarity on a map table dissolve, on contact with the enemy, into a chaos of contradictory reports, delayed messages and simple human error. The armies that win are rarely the ones with the most elegant plan; they are the ones whose soldiers and junior officers can improvise competently when that plan, as it always does, begins to fall apart. This is why military academies the world over spend as much time training judgement and initiative at the lowest ranks as they do teaching the formal theory of strategy. A private who can think for himself when his section commander falls is worth more, in the moment that matters, than an elegant plan nobody left alive can execute.

questions.stem: S1. A young officer's first command is rarely glamorous.
subs: P: It usually involves managing rations, resolving petty disputes and inspecting equipment.

S: Textbooks rarely mention this, but veteran officers insist it is the real training ground.
S6. Command, in other words, is learned in the details long before it is exercised in crisis.

questions.direction: S1 and S6 are fixed. The middle four sentences P, Q, R, S are jumbled. Choose the option that gives the correct sequence.

questions.stem: S1. The printing press changed the course of human history within a few generations.
subs: P: Ideas that once travelled at the speed of a horse could now spread within weeks.
Q: Books, once rare and expensive, became affordable to ordinary readers.
R: Religious and political authorities lost their monopoly over information.
S: Literacy rates rose sharply across Europe as a direct consequence.
S6. Few inventions since have matched its effect on the structure of society.
questions.subject: Ordering of Sentences / Para-jumbles
questions.direction: S1 and S6 are fixed. The middle four sentences P, Q, R, S are jumbled. Choose the option that gives the correct sequence.

questions.stem: S1. Water scarcity in urban India is often described as a supply problem.
subs: P: In truth, most cities receive enough rainfall to meet their annual needs.
Q: What they lack is the infrastructure to capture and store it efficiently.
R: Ageing pipelines lose a significant share of treated water before it reaches homes.
S: The result is an artificial scarcity created by poor management, not by nature.

questions.subject: Ordering of Sentences / Para-jumbles
questions.direction: S1 and S6 are fixed. The middle four sentences P, Q, R, S are jumbled. Choose the option that gives the correct sequence.

questions.stem: S1. Teamwork under pressure looks very different from teamwork in a classroom exercise.
subs: P: Under real pressure, roles blur and every member must be ready to step up.
Q: There is little time for lengthy discussion or consensus-building.
R: Trust built beforehand becomes the only currency that matters.
S: Decisions must be made quickly, often on incomplete information.
S6. This is why military training emphasises drills over theory: instinct must replace deliberation.
questions.subject: Ordering of Sentences / Para-jumbles
questions.direction: S1 and S6 are fixed. The middle four sentences P, Q, R, S are jumbled. Choose the option that gives the correct sequence.

questions.stem: S1. History remembers few battles won by superior numbers alone.
subs: P: Far more often, victory belonged to the side with better intelligence.
Q: Knowing the terrain, the enemy's supply lines and morale mattered more than headcount.
R: Commanders who understood this invested heavily in scouting and reconnaissance.
S: Those who ignored it paid the price, however large their armies.
S6. Modern warfare, for all its technology, has only sharpened this old lesson.
questions.subject: Ordering of Sentences / Para-jumbles
questions.direction: S1 and S6 are fixed. The middle four sentences P, Q, R, S are jumbled. Choose the option that gives the correct sequence.

questions.stem: S1. Every profession has its own definition of a 'good day at work'.
subs: P: For a soldier on the border, it might simply mean a quiet, uneventful shift.
Q: For a surgeon, it might mean an operation that goes exactly to plan.
R: For a teacher, it might mean a single student finally understanding a difficult idea.
S: What unites these very different definitions is a sense of quiet, unspectacular competence.
S6. Success, in most serious professions, rarely announces itself with fanfare.
questions.subject: Ordering of Sentences / Para-jumbles
questions.direction: S1 and S6 are fixed. The middle four sentences P, Q, R, S are jumbled. Choose the option that gives the correct sequence.

questions.stem: S1. The habit of reading widely is often undervalued in career advice.
subs: P: Yet it quietly builds a store of ideas that no single course can teach.
Q: A well-read officer draws on history, literature and science to solve unfamiliar problems.
R: This breadth becomes most valuable precisely when a situation has no textbook answer.
S: Narrow expertise, by contrast, can leave a person helpless outside its boundaries.
S6. This is why the best training academies still insist on a broad, liberal curriculum.
questions.subject: Ordering of Sentences / Para-jumbles
questions.direction: S1 and S6 are fixed. The middle four sentences P, Q, R, S are jumbled. Choose the option that gives the correct sequence.

questions.stem: S1. Punctuality is often dismissed as a minor virtue compared to competence or courage.
subs: P: But a person who is habitually late is quietly telling others their time does not matter.
Q: Over time, this erodes trust far more than a single dramatic failure would.

S: Armies have long understood this, which is why timing is drilled relentlessly.
S6. Small disciplines, repeated daily, are what larger disciplines are ultimately built from.
